messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezoelectric energy harvester (sinusoidal current source $I_p$, capacitance $C_p$, leakage $R_{leak}$).
    *   Load $R_L$ from `out` to ground.
    *   Goal: $1.8\text{V} \le V_{out} \le 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$.
    *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
    *   Stability $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Operating conditions S1-S6 vary $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, and $R_L$.
    *   Key constraints: $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$. Diode drops are significant.
    *   Reference Design (Full-bridge rectifier) failed on S2 (heavy load), S3 (overvoltage), and S4 (weak excitation).

    *   The open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2 \pi f C_p)$ is around $3.2\text{V}$.
    *   Standard Bridge Rectifier (FBR) has two diode drops ($\sim 0.5\text{V}$ each), meaning the output voltage is limited.
    *   S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation) failed $V_{out\_min}$, suggesting a need for higher efficiency or a voltage boost.
    *   S3 (strong excitation, light load) failed $V_{out\_max}$, suggesting a need for overvoltage protection (Zener clamp).
    *   S5 (low freq) failed $dv$, suggesting potential stability or ripple issues.

    *   *Topology 1: Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) or similar.* This is the gold standard for piezo harvesting. It uses an inductor to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the extracted energy.
    *   *Topology 2: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge).* Replaces diodes with switches to reduce voltage drops.
    *   *Topology 3: Half-bridge or Charge Pump.* Using capacitors to boost voltage.
    *   *Topology 4: Simple Bridge with Zener Clamp.* To fix S3's overvoltage.

    *   **Design A: SSHI (Simplified)**
        *   Basically, we use a switch and an inductor to invert the charge on $C_p$ at the peaks.
        *   Circuit: Piezo $\to$ Bridge $\to$ Out. But we add the flipping mechanism.
        *   Actually, a simpler "Parallel-SSHI" or "Series-SSHI" can be complex. Let's try a basic inductor-based inversion if possible.
        *   Wait, looking at the "Components you may use" section, I have `S` (switch) and `SYNC`.
        *   A standard SSHI: Inductor $L$ in series with a switch $S$. When $V_{pzp}$ reaches a peak, $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, and the voltage flips.
        *   Circuit structure: $L$ between `pzp` and `n1`, $S$ between `n1` and `pzn`. `SYNC` triggers at peaks. Then a rectifier to `out`.

    *   **Design B: Full-Bridge Rectifier with Zener Clamp**
        *   Start with FBR, add a `DZ33` Zener diode from `out` to `0`.
        *   This solves S3 (vmax) but doesn't fix S2/S4 (vmin). However, it's a baseline.

    *   **Design C: Synchronous Rectification (Active Bridge)**
        *   The `S` components are ideal switches. If we can implement a bridge with switches, we eliminate diode drops.
        *   But `SYNC` only works at "piezo voltage extrema".
        *   Let's try a half-wave synchronous rectifier or a variation.

    *   *Refining SSHI (Design A):*
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        *   L1: [pzp, n1]
        *   S1: [n1, pzn]
        *   SYNC G1: edges="both", phase=0.0. (Closes S1 at peaks to flip $C_p$ voltage).
        *   Wait, the bridge is still needed to move the energy to `out`.
        *   Rectifier: D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out], D3[0, pzp], D4[0, pzn] ? No, that's a bridge.
        *   Actually, if I use a bridge *and* the SSHI flip, I get much more power.
        *   Let's try:
            *   Cout: [out, 0]
            *   Bridge: D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out], D3[0, pzp], D4[0, pzn] (wait, anodes/cathodes: D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out], D3[0, pzp], D4[0, pzn] is wrong).
            *   Standard bridge: D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out], D3[0, pzp], D4[0, pzn]... No.
            *   Standard: D1[pzp, out], D2[pzn, out], D3[0, pzp], D4[0, pzn]... let's be careful.
            *   Full Bridge nodes:
                1. [pzp, out] (DSCH)
                2. [pzn, out] (DSCH) - *Wait, these can't both be anodes to out.*
                *Correct Bridge:*
                - D1: [pzp, out]
                - D2: [pzn, out] ... no.
                - D1: [pzp, n_rect]
                - D2: [pzn, n_rect] ... no.
                - *Correct Full Bridge:*
                    D1: [pzp, out]
                    D2: [pzn, out] --- no.
                    Let's use:
                    D1: [pzp, out]
                    D2: [pzn, out] --- no.
                    If I want `out` to be positive:
                    - Path 1: pzp -> out (D1)
                    - Path 2: pzn -> out (D2) --- No, when pzp is positive, pzn is negative.
                    - Correct:
                        D1: [pzp, out]
                        D2: [pzn, out] (Wait, this is wrong).
                        Let's use the reference design's bridge:
                        D1: ["pzp", "out"]
                        D2: ["pzn", "out"] (No, the reference says "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]". Let me re-read).
                        "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have their anode on ground)".
                        Wait:
                        D1: pzp -> out
                        D2: pzn -> out (This only works if pzn is positive)
                        D3: 0 -> pzp (Anode 0, Cathode pzp)
                        D4: 0 -> pzn (Anode 0, Cathode pzn)
                        This is a standard bridge. When pzp is +, current flows pzp -> out -> load -> 0 -> pzn. When pzn is +, current flows pzn -> out -> load -> 0 -> pzp.

    *   *Refining the SSHI implementation:*
        *   Piezo terminals: pzp, pzn.
        *   Flip circuit: L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn].
        *   Rectifier: D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn].
        *   Storage: C1 [out, 0].
        *   Zener: D5 [0, out] (DZ33).
        *   Sync: G1 (edges="both").
        *   Wait, the flip happens at the peaks of the voltage. The piezo current is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$. Voltage is $V_{oc} \cos(\omega t)$. Zero crossing of current is the peak of voltage. `SYNC` closes at current zero crossings. Perfect.

    *   **Design A: SSHI + Bridge + Zener**
        *   Flipping: L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 [edges="both", ton=...].
        *   Rectification: D1-D4 (Full Bridge).
        *   Output: C1 [out, 0], D5 [0, out] (Zener).
        *   This should increase the voltage harvested (fixing S2/S4) and clamp the maximum (fixing S3).

    *   **Design B: Simple Bridge + Zener (Baseline for S3)**
        *   Just the FBR + Zener. It fixes S3 but likely fails S2/S4. However, it's a safe bet if SSHI is too aggressive.

    *   **Design C: Half-Wave Rectifier with Active Switch**
        *   Instead of a bridge, use one diode and one switch.
        *   S1: [pzp, out], G1 [edges="pos", phase=0].
        *   D1: [out, pzn] (Wait, that's not right).
        *   Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" (using switches instead of diodes).
        *   S1: [pzp, out], G1 [edges="pos"].
        *   S2: [pzn, out], G2 [edges="neg"].
        *   D3: [0, pzp] (Wait, we need return paths).
        *   S3: [0, pzp], G1 [edges="pos"].
        *   S4: [0, pzn], G2 [edges="neg"].
        *   This removes the diode drop entirely.
        *   Actually, let's stick to a simpler "Active Bridge" if possible, but `S` components are limited to 4.
        *   A full active bridge uses 4 switches.
        *   S1: [pzp, out], S2: [pzn, out], S3: [0, pzp], S4: [0, pzn].
        *   G1 (pos): closes S1 and S4.
        *   G2 (neg): closes S2 and S3.
        *   This would have 0V drop.

    *   *Option 1: SSHI + Bridge + Zener.* (Very powerful, standard for high efficiency).
    *   *Option 2: Full Active Bridge + Zener.* (Zero drop, fixes S2/S4, fixes S3).
    *   *Option 3: Bridge + Zener (Standard).* (Conservative).

    *Wait, for the Active Bridge (Option 2):*
    *   S1 [pzp, out], S2 [pzn, out], S3 [0, pzp], S4 [0, pzn].
    *   G1: edges="pos", phase=0.0. (S1 and S4)
    *   G2: edges="neg", phase=0.0. (S2 and S3)
    *   This replaces 4 diodes with 4 switches. This should significantly help S2 and S4.

    *Let's refine the SSHI (Option 1) again:*
    *   SSHI needs the inductor to be in parallel with the piezo during the flip.
    *   The flip circuit: L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn].
    *   When S1 closes, L1 is in parallel with (pzp-pzn).
    *   Wait, the bridge is still there. Will the bridge interfere with the flip?
    *   Yes, the diodes will conduct. The inductor $L$ must be small enough to flip the voltage quickly, and $t_{on}$ must be short.
    *   The bridge: D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn].
    *   If $V_{pzp}$ is high, D1 conducts. If we then close S1, L1 and $C_p$ will oscillate.
    *   Actually, the standard SSHI (Parallel) is:
        Piezo terminals pzp, pzn.
        S1 [pzp, n1], L1 [n1, pzn]. (Flip circuit).
        And then a rectifier from pzp, pzn to `out`.
        This is what I have.

    *   S2 (Heavy Load): $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$. Bridge voltage drop (0.5V) is a huge percentage of $V_{oc}=3.2\text{V}$.
    *   S4 (Weak Excitation): $I_p = 30\mu\text{A}$. Again, diode drop is the enemy.
    *   S3 (Light Load): $R_L = 2200\text{k}\Omega$. Output voltage will climb. Needs clamping.

    *   Let's propose:
        1.  `active_bridge`: 4 switches (S1-S4), 2 SYNCs (G1, G2), 1 Zener, 1 Cap.
        2.  `sshi_bridge`: 1 inductor (L1), 1 switch (S1), 1 SYNC (G1), 4 diodes (D1-D4), 1 Zener (D5), 1 Cap (C1).
        3.  `fbr_zener`: 4 diodes (D1-D4), 1 Zener (D5), 1 Cap (C1).

    *   *Wait, let's double check the Active Bridge connectivity:*
        S1: [pzp, out] (closes when pzp > 0)
        S2: [pzn, out] (closes when pzn > 0)
        S3: [0, pzp] (closes when pzp < 0)
        S4: [0, pzn] (closes when pzn < 0)
        G1 (pos): triggers S1 and S4. (pzp +, pzn -)
        G2 (neg): triggers S2 and S3. (pzp -, pzn +)
        *Correction:* S4 should close when pzn < 0? No, the path is pzp(+) -> out -> load -> 0 -> pzn(-).
        So:
        G1 (pos): closes S1 [pzp, out] and S4 [0, pzn].
        G2 (neg): closes S2 [pzn, out] and S3 [0, pzp].
        This is a perfect active bridge.

    *   *Let's double check the SSHI connectivity:*
        L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 [edges="both"].
        Bridge: D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn].
        C1 [out, 0], D5 [0, out].
        This is also strong.

    *   *Let's double check the FBR_Zener connectivity:*
        D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn].
        C1 [out, 0], D5 [0, out].

    *   `active_bridge`:
        S1 [pzp, out], ctrl: G1
        S2 [pzn, out], ctrl: G2
        S3 [0, pzp], ctrl: G2
        S4 [0, pzn], ctrl: G1
        G1: edges="pos", phase=0.0, ton=...
        G2: edges="neg", phase=0.0, ton=...
        *Wait, `ton` for a rectifier should be long!* The `SYNC` controller closes switches for `ton` seconds. If `ton` is 1ms (the max), that's only 1/100th of the period.
        *Critical Realization:* The `S` switch in this environment is ONLY closed for `ton` duration. It's a pulse, not a half-cycle.
        Therefore, the "Active Bridge" as I designed it won't work because it only conducts for `ton` seconds. It would be a switched-capacitor converter, not a rectifier.

    *   *Back to the drawing board:*
        If `S` is only for pulses, then `S` is meant for SSHI (flipping) or for some kind of switched-mode power supply.
        For rectification, I *must* use diodes `D`.

    *   *Re-evaluating SSHI:*
        In SSHI, the flip is a short pulse.
        The rectification is done by diodes.
        So, SSHI + Bridge + Zener is a very viable topology.

    *   *What about the "Active Bridge" then?*
        If I want to replace the diodes, I can't use `S` unless I can keep it closed. But `S` is controlled by `SYNC`, which is pulse-based.
        Wait, the prompt says: "`SYNC` closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
        This means `S` is definitely for pulses.

    *   *Wait, if `S` is only for pulses, how can we fix the diode drop for S2 and S4?*
        Maybe a charge pump?
        A Dickson charge pump uses diodes and capacitors.
        Or, the SSHI itself increases the voltage *before* the bridge.
        By flipping the voltage, SSHI effectively increases the voltage across the diodes, making them conduct more and increasing the overall efficiency.

    *   *Let's look at the SSHI again:*
        Piezo $C_p$ is $25\text{nF}$. $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$.
        If we flip the voltage at the peak, we can potentially double the voltage across the bridge.
        The `S` switch closes for `ton`. For L-Cp inversion, $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        $L = 1\text{mH}, C_p = 25\text{nF} \implies t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-3} \times 25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 3.14 \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \approx 15.7\mu\text{s}$.
        This fits within the `ton` range (100ns to 1ms).

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI_Bridge**
        *   L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 [edges="both", ton=1e-05]
        *   D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn] (FBR)
        *   C1 [out, 0], D5 [0, out] (Zener)
        *   Rationale: SSHI increases the energy extracted from the piezo by flipping the voltage at peaks, helping with S2/S4. Zener clamp fixes S3.

    *   **Proposal 2: Half-Wave_SSHI**
        *   L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, pzn], G1 [edges="both", ton=1e-05]
        *   D1 [pzp, out], C1 [out, 0], D5 [0, out] (Zener)
        *   Wait, this is just a half-wave. Maybe a full-bridge is better.
        *   Let's try a different variant of SSHI: The "Series-SSHI".
        *   Actually, let's try a "Voltage Doubler" (Charge Pump).
        *   C_pump [pzp, n1], D1 [n1, out], D2 [pzn, 0]... No, that's for AC.
        *   Let's try:
            D1 [pzp, n1]
            C1 [n1, 0]
            D2 [n1, out] (No, that doesn't work)
            *Standard Doubler:*
            C1 [pzp, n1], D1 [n1, 0]
            C2 [n1, out], D2 [pzp, out]
            This is also not quite right for a piezo.

    *   **Proposal 3: FBR_Zener** (The basic fix for S3)
        *   D1 [pzp, out], D2 [pzn, out], D3 [0, pzp], D4 [0, pzn]
        *   C1 [out, 0], D5 [0, out]
        *   Rationale: Simple bridge with a Zener clamp to ensure $V_{out}$ never exceeds 3.6V, addressing S3.

    *   *One more thought:* Could we use the `S` switch to implement a buck-boost converter?
        *   L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, 0], G1 [edges="pos"].
        *   D1 [n1, out], C1 [out, 0].
        *   This would be a boost converter. When S1 closes, L1 charges from pzp. When S1 opens, L1 discharges into `out` via D1.
        *   This could significantly boost the voltage for S2 and S4.
        *   Let's refine this "Boost" topology:
            L1 [pzp, n1], S1 [n1, 0], G1 [edges="both", ton=...]. (Using "both" to charge from both polarity).
            Wait, if G1 is "both", it closes when pzp is + and when pzp is -.
            If pzp is +, L1 charges. If pzp is -, L1 charges (since it's now pzp(-) to 0).
            D1 [n1, out], C1 [out, 0], D5 [0, out] (Zener).
            This is a very efficient way to boost voltage.

    *   *Comparing SSHI vs Boost:*
        *   SSHI flips the voltage across $C_p$, which is a very specific piezo technique.
        *   Boost converter (L-S-D) is a general power electronics technique.
        *   Given the components, a Boost might be easier to tune.
        *   Let's propose the Boost as Proposal 2.

    *   S1: pzp-n1, S1: n1-0, G1: both.
    *   Wait, if $V_{pzp}$ is negative, L1 will charge but the current will flow from 0 to pzp.
    *   When S1 opens, L1 will try to push current to `out` via D1.
    *   But the voltage at `n1` during the open phase will be $V_{pzp} + V_{L1}$.
    *   Since $V_{pzp}$ is sinusoidal, $V_{pzp}$ will be negative half the time.
    *   This means the Boost only works effectively during the positive half-cycle.
    *   To use both half-cycles, we'd need a rectifier *before* the boost or a more complex switching scheme.
